evidence: Ter. Ph. 193: nescio quod magnum hoc nūntiō exspectō malum
terms.comment: “What’s the trouble?”: Quid istuc malī est? (Ter. Ph. 184, Heaut. 82; Plaut. Merc. 165); Traupman (p. 110) also gives Quid est negōtī? (see problem). To make trouble for someone, that is, punish him: malum dare alicui (Traupman 110).

terms.gloss: be in trouble, be in difficulties
evidence: Cic. Att. 4.1.3: in rē autem familiārī … valdē labōrāmus
terms.comment: With in and the ablative of the matter; also of being ill (see suffer, from an illness).

evidence: Cic. Att. 11.3.3: is quoque in angustiīs est quīcum sumus
Traupman 105: to be in a pickle, in angustiīs versor

terms.gloss: have one’s hands full, be hard pressed
evidence: Gell. 3.8.1: satisque agerent Rōmānī (Lewis & Short s.v. satis)
Cic. Att. 4.15.9: pugnātur ācriter: agitur tamen satis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to have enough to do, have one’s hands full; to be in trouble”. Impersonal, agitur satis, it is a hard struggle. Traupman 99 gives agitur satis for “things are going fairly well”, which it does not mean (see so-so).

phrases.latin: Nescio quod magnum hoc nūntiō exspectō malum.
phrases.english: With this news I expect some big trouble.

phrases.latin: in rē autem familiārī, quae quem ad modum frācta, dissipāta, dīrepta sit nōn ignōrās, valdē labōrāmus
phrases.english: but with my money, which, as you know, has been broken up, scattered and plundered, I am in real trouble
To make big trouble for someone.
in a pinch (in a doubtful situation)
